subject: Core Mathematics
sourceNote: We located the genuine 2024-edition KICD 'Grade 10 Core Mathematics Curriculum Design' PDF (13.3MB, 69 pages) at a third-party teacher resource mirror, but it is a scanned image document with no extractable text layer (confirmed via pdftotext: zero characters recovered) and OCR tooling was not available in the build environment within the time budget. Strand naming below follows the standard CBE Grade 10 Mathematics structure reported by multiple teacher-resource sites. Sub-strand detail (learning outcomes, board notes, activity, assessment questions) is illustrative content written in the style of a KICD curriculum design, NOT verbatim official text. Replace this file with the real KICD PDF's extracted/OCR'd text when available; the app's pack-assembly logic does not change.

subStrands.citation: Grade 10 Core Mathematics Curriculum Design — Strand: Sequences and Series — Sub-strand: Arithmetic Sequences (illustrative; verify against official KICD PDF)
learningOutcomes: Identify the common difference of an arithmetic sequence
Find the nth term of an arithmetic sequence
Calculate the sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic series
boardNotes: Arithmetic sequence: each term = previous term + constant difference (d)
nth term: Tn = a + (n-1)d,  where a = first term
Sum of first n terms: Sn = n/2 [2a + (n-1)d]

activity.description: Learners each count off a number in a line (1,2,3...), then the class builds a real arithmetic sequence by skip-counting (e.g. by 3s) out loud, identifying a and d before finding T10 together.

assessmentQuestions.question: What is the common difference of 4, 7, 10, 13?
Find the 6th term of the sequence 2, 5, 8, 11, ...
assessmentQuestions.markingScheme: 2 marks for 17 with formula shown; 1 mark for correct method, arithmetic slip.

assessmentQuestions.question: Write the formula for the nth term of an arithmetic sequence.
Find the sum of the first 5 terms of 3, 6, 9, 12, 15.
assessmentQuestions.markingScheme: 2 marks for 45; 1 mark for correct setup with an arithmetic error.

assessmentQuestions.question: A sequence has a = 5 and d = -2. Find the 4th term.
assessmentQuestions.markingScheme: 2 marks for -1; 1 mark for correct substitution with a sign error.

subStrands.explainer: An arithmetic sequence just keeps adding (or subtracting) the same number each time. If you know the first term and how much it changes by each step, you can jump straight to any term without listing them all — that's what the nth-term formula does.

subStrands.citation: Grade 10 Core Mathematics Curriculum Design — Strand: Sequences and Series — Sub-strand: Geometric Sequences (illustrative; verify against official KICD PDF)
learningOutcomes: Identify the common ratio of a geometric sequence
Find the nth term of a geometric sequence
Calculate the sum of the first n terms of a geometric series
boardNotes: Geometric sequence: each term = previous term x constant ratio (r)
Sum of first n terms (r != 1): Sn = a(1 - r^n) / (1 - r)

activity.description: Tell the classic 'rice grains doubling on a chessboard' story (1,2,4,8...) and have learners predict how large the number gets by square 10 versus square 20, then check with the formula.

assessmentQuestions.question: What is the common ratio of 2, 6, 18, 54?
Find the 5th term of the sequence 3, 6, 12, 24, ...
assessmentQuestions.markingScheme: 2 marks for 48; 1 mark for correct method, arithmetic slip.

assessmentQuestions.question: Write the formula for the nth term of a geometric sequence.
A sequence has a = 2 and r = 3. Find the 4th term.
assessmentQuestions.markingScheme: 2 marks for 54; 1 mark for correct substitution with an arithmetic error.

assessmentQuestions.question: Explain in one sentence why geometric growth eventually outpaces arithmetic growth.
assessmentQuestions.markingScheme: 2 marks for referencing repeated multiplication vs repeated addition; 1 mark for a vaguer 'it grows faster' answer.

subStrands.explainer: A geometric sequence keeps multiplying by the same number. This is why it grows much faster than an arithmetic sequence — doubling something ten times gives you far more than adding the same amount ten times.
